title: SysDesign Quest: system design learning expansion

items.title: DNS, TCP, and TLS: follow a request
items.summary: Opening a website resembles finding an office, establishing a conversation, and checking whom you are speaking to.
objectives: Trace a new HTTPS connection from name lookup to response.
Separate name resolution, transport reliability, and transport security.
Explain why a network timeout does not prove an operation failed.

questions.prompt: Does a TCP acknowledgement prove an order was saved?
questions.answer: No. It acknowledges transport receipt, not successful application processing or durable commit.
questions.explanation: No. It acknowledges transport receipt, not successful application processing or durable commit.

questions.prompt: Why can users reach the old server after a DNS update?
questions.answer: Cached records and established connections may continue using the old destination; changing authoritative DNS does not revoke them.
questions.explanation: Cached records and established connections may continue using the old destination; changing authoritative DNS does not revoke them.

items.title: HTTP and API design: define the contract
items.summary: An API is a promise about what a caller may ask, what the server changes, and what a response means.
objectives: Choose a method and response contract for a resource.
Distinguish safe methods from idempotent operations.
Use conditional updates to detect conflicting edits.

questions.prompt: Can repeated DELETE requests be idempotent if the second returns 404?
questions.answer: Yes. Idempotence concerns intended state effects, not identical status codes.
questions.explanation: Yes. Idempotence concerns intended state effects, not identical status codes.

questions.prompt: Does 202 mean that the requested report exists?
questions.answer: No. It means processing was accepted; completion needs a separate observation.
questions.explanation: No. It means processing was accepted; completion needs a separate observation.

items.title: Latency, throughput, and queueing
items.summary: A restaurant can serve many meals per hour while making each customer wait a long time.
objectives: Separate response time, service time, arrival rate, and completion rate.
Calculate average in-flight work using Little's Law.
Recognize when averages conceal slow user experiences.

questions.prompt: At 50 requests/s and 0.2 s mean latency, what is average concurrency?
questions.answer: 10 requests, if the measured system is stable and the throughput and latency refer to the same boundary.
questions.explanation: 10 requests, if the measured system is stable and the throughput and latency refer to the same boundary.

questions.prompt: Why can CPU be low while requests time out?
questions.answer: Requests may be waiting on locks, connections, network responses, or queues instead of consuming CPU.
questions.explanation: Requests may be waiting on locks, connections, network responses, or queues instead of consuming CPU.

items.title: Concurrency, parallelism, and shared state
items.summary: Concurrency means several tasks are in progress during overlapping periods.
objectives: Distinguish concurrent progress from simultaneous execution.
Demonstrate a lost update with an execution timeline.
Choose bounded work and an appropriate synchronization boundary.

questions.prompt: Does adding await make a CPU-heavy loop run in parallel?
questions.answer: No. It enables suspension at appropriate operations; CPU parallelism requires an execution model that supports it.
questions.explanation: No. It enables suspension at appropriate operations; CPU parallelism requires an execution model that supports it.

questions.prompt: When is a local mutex insufficient for an inventory rule?
questions.answer: When other processes or services can update the same inventory without participating in that mutex.
questions.explanation: When other processes or services can update the same inventory without participating in that mutex.

items.title: Indexes and query plans: read less data
items.summary: An index is an alternate route to data, like a book's index of terms.
objectives: Derive an index candidate from filters and ordering.
Read estimated versus actual plan information.
Explain why an index can slow writes or be ignored.

questions.prompt: Why might a sequential scan be the right plan?
questions.answer: If a query needs much of the table, reading it sequentially can cost less than many index-guided table reads.
questions.explanation: If a query needs much of the table, reading it sequentially can cost less than many index-guided table reads.

questions.prompt: Is EXPLAIN ANALYZE a read-only inspection command for any SQL statement?
questions.answer: No. It executes the statement. Treat writes and side-effecting functions accordingly.
questions.explanation: No. It executes the statement. Treat writes and side-effecting functions accordingly.

items.title: Requirements and capacity: turn assumptions into numbers
items.summary: A design begins with questions about the product.
objectives: Separate user behavior, invariants, and performance targets.
Estimate traffic, storage, and bandwidth with stated units.
Identify which assumption could change the architecture.

questions.prompt: Is 'one million registered users' enough for a capacity estimate?
questions.answer: No. You need activity, actions per active user, timing, payloads, and retention assumptions.
questions.explanation: No. You need activity, actions per active user, timing, payloads, and retention assumptions.

questions.prompt: Which assumption changes first when a flash crowd appears?
questions.answer: The peak arrival pattern and concurrency; the registered-user count may remain unchanged.
questions.explanation: The peak arrival pattern and concurrency; the registered-user count may remain unchanged.

items.title: Load balancing, health checks, and draining
items.summary: A load balancer chooses where work goes.
objectives: Choose connection-level or request-level routing for a workload.
Separate readiness, liveness, and startup checks.
Describe how to remove an instance without abandoning requests.

questions.prompt: Should a database slowdown always fail application liveness?
questions.answer: No. Restarting healthy application processes may worsen a shared dependency incident.
questions.explanation: No. Restarting healthy application processes may worsen a shared dependency incident.

questions.prompt: Does equal connection count imply equal request load?
questions.answer: No. Connections can differ greatly in request count, duration, and resource cost.
questions.explanation: No. Connections can differ greatly in request count, duration, and resource cost.

items.title: Caching, invalidation, and stampedes
items.summary: A cache keeps a reusable copy closer to the reader or cheaper to retrieve.
objectives: Choose a cache key, freshness policy, and authority.
Explain a stale refill race and a cache stampede.
Estimate origin demand from hit rate and misses.

questions.prompt: Does a 30-second TTL alone guarantee every served value is at most 30 seconds behind the authority?
questions.answer: No. Delayed fills, stale upstream reads, and refresh behavior can make the original data older than the entry's lifetime.
questions.explanation: No. Delayed fills, stale upstream reads, and refresh behavior can make the original data older than the entry's lifetime.

questions.prompt: What does HTTP no-cache mean?
questions.answer: A stored response requires validation before reuse; it is not the same as no-store.
questions.explanation: A stored response requires validation before reuse; it is not the same as no-store.

items.title: Connection pooling and resource budgets
items.summary: A pool reuses a limited number of established connections.
objectives: Budget connections across every process and replica.
Distinguish pool waiting from database execution.
Choose a pooling mode compatible with application state.

questions.prompt: Does a pool timeout prove the database query ran slowly?
questions.answer: No. The request may never have obtained a connection or submitted a query.
questions.explanation: No. The request may never have obtained a connection or submitted a query.

questions.prompt: Why include deployment overlap in connection budgets?
questions.answer: Old and new instances may run together, multiplying potential connections before the old fleet drains.
questions.explanation: Old and new instances may run together, multiplying potential connections before the old fleet drains.

items.title: Queues and background jobs
items.summary: A queue decouples accepting work from performing it.
objectives: Separate durable acceptance from successful completion.
Place acknowledgements relative to business effects.
Estimate backlog growth and recovery capacity.

questions.prompt: Does a publisher confirm mean the report has been generated?
questions.answer: No. It concerns publication, not successful consumer-side report generation.
questions.explanation: No. It concerns publication, not successful consumer-side report generation.

questions.prompt: Why is oldest-job age a useful metric?
questions.answer: It directly exposes how long accepted work has waited, while count alone ignores job cost and arrival patterns.
questions.explanation: It directly exposes how long accepted work has waited, while count alone ignores job cost and arrival patterns.

items.title: Object storage, delivery, and CDNs
items.summary: Large files are often better addressed as objects than stored inside application rows.
objectives: Separate binary objects from transactional metadata.
Design an upload and publish sequence.
Explain why storage consistency and CDN freshness differ.

questions.prompt: Does a strongly consistent object store guarantee fresh CDN responses?
questions.answer: No. The CDN can retain a previously fetched representation under its independent cache policy.
questions.explanation: No. The CDN can retain a previously fetched representation under its independent cache policy.

questions.prompt: Why keep an upload record in a pending state?
questions.answer: It separates successful byte transfer from validation and publication, and makes incomplete workflows recoverable.
questions.explanation: It separates successful byte transfer from validation and publication, and makes incomplete workflows recoverable.

items.title: Pagination and data access patterns
items.summary: Pagination is a contract for continuing through a collection.
objectives: Compare offset pagination with keyset pagination.
Define a total ordering and cursor contract.
Explain why a cursor is not automatically a snapshot.

questions.prompt: Why is created_at alone often an insufficient cursor key?
questions.answer: Several rows can share that value, so a unique tiebreaker is needed to continue without ambiguity.
questions.explanation: Several rows can share that value, so a unique tiebreaker is needed to continue without ambiguity.

questions.prompt: Does keyset pagination guarantee an immutable result set?
questions.answer: No. It defines continuation; concurrent updates, deletions, and snapshot policy still determine visibility.
questions.explanation: No. It defines continuation; concurrent updates, deletions, and snapshot policy still determine visibility.

items.title: Partitioning, hot keys, and consistent hashing
items.summary: Partitioning splits one dataset across several nodes so that each node stores and serves only part of it.
objectives: Choose hash or range partitioning from a stated access pattern.
Calculate how many keys move when a node joins or leaves, under hash mod N and under consistent hashing.
Explain why a hot key needs a workload change rather than rebalancing.

questions.prompt: Does consistent hashing stop a single hot key from overloading its node?
questions.answer: No. It decides which node owns each key, and every request for that key still goes to that owner. Spreading one key's load needs a workload change, such as caching its reads or splitting it into sub-keys.
questions.explanation: No. It decides which node owns each key, and every request for that key still goes to that owner. Spreading one key's load needs a workload change, such as caching its reads or splitting it into sub-keys.

questions.prompt: Why do virtual nodes help when a node fails?
questions.answer: Each physical node holds many small arcs of the ring, so a failed node's keys scatter across many survivors instead of all landing on one neighbor.
questions.explanation: Each physical node holds many small arcs of the ring, so a failed node's keys scatter across many survivors instead of all landing on one neighbor.

items.title: Timeouts, retries, and jitter
items.summary: A timeout is the caller deciding it has waited long enough.
objectives: Allocate an end-to-end deadline across attempts and waiting.
Explain retry amplification across service layers.
Choose retry eligibility, limits, and randomized delays.

questions.prompt: If every layer retries three times, is the deepest service called only three times?
questions.answer: No. Nested attempts can multiply; three layers with three attempts each can produce 27 calls.
questions.explanation: No. Nested attempts can multiply; three layers with three attempts each can produce 27 calls.

questions.prompt: Does a timeout authorize treating a payment as failed?
questions.answer: No. The operation may have committed; inspect durable state or reconcile using the original operation identity.
questions.explanation: No. The operation may have committed; inspect durable state or reconcile using the original operation identity.

items.title: Idempotency and deduplication
items.summary: A duplicate request should mean 'continue or return the same operation,' not 'perform a new operation that happens to look similar.' Idempotency turns ambiguous retries into a protocol with a stable identity.
objectives: Define idempotency key scope, retention, and payload matching.
Make duplicate claims and local effects atomic.
Identify the boundary where an external effect escapes a transaction.

questions.prompt: Is a content hash always a valid substitute for a client operation key?
questions.answer: No. Two intentionally separate operations may have identical payloads.
questions.explanation: No. Two intentionally separate operations may have identical payloads.

questions.prompt: Why must retention be documented?
questions.answer: The duplicate-suppression guarantee only covers the period and scope for which identifying state remains available.
questions.explanation: The duplicate-suppression guarantee only covers the period and scope for which identifying state remains available.

items.title: Delivery guarantees and ordering
items.summary: A message has several lives: it is published, stored, delivered, processed, and turned into an effect.
objectives: Trace the commit/acknowledgement ambiguity.
State the boundary of an exactly-once claim.
Choose ordering scope and handle repeated or stale events.

questions.prompt: Does transactional Kafka processing automatically make an external SQL update exactly once?
questions.answer: No. The external effect needs its own coordinated or idempotent commit strategy.
questions.explanation: No. The external effect needs its own coordinated or idempotent commit strategy.

questions.prompt: Can messages delivered in order produce effects out of order?
questions.answer: Yes. Concurrent workers, retries, and differing execution times can change completion order.
questions.explanation: Yes. Concurrent workers, retries, and differing execution times can change completion order.

items.title: Transactional outbox and change data capture
items.summary: An order update and its notification are often stored in different systems.
objectives: Identify the failure gap in a database-plus-broker dual write.
Design an atomic outbox record and replayable publication.
Separate database changes from stable domain events.

questions.prompt: Does the outbox remove duplicate event delivery?
questions.answer: No. It removes the local dual-write gap; relays can republish after uncertain outcomes.
questions.explanation: No. It removes the local dual-write gap; relays can republish after uncertain outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why store an event schema version?
questions.answer: Consumers need a stable way to interpret payloads as producers evolve independently.
questions.explanation: Consumers need a stable way to interpret payloads as producers evolve independently.

items.title: Sagas and compensating actions
items.summary: A workflow spanning independently owned services rarely fits into one local transaction.
objectives: Model a workflow as durable local transitions.
Separate compensation from transaction rollback.
Handle timeout, retry, and manual-repair states explicitly.

questions.prompt: Does compensation restore every outside observer to the original state?
questions.answer: No. Effects such as notifications, fees, and observations may be irreversible.
questions.explanation: No. Effects such as notifications, fees, and observations may be irreversible.

questions.prompt: Why persist the coordinator's state?
questions.answer: A restarted coordinator must resume or repair the workflow without forgetting completed steps or issuing contradictory actions.
questions.explanation: A restarted coordinator must resume or repair the workflow without forgetting completed steps or issuing contradictory actions.

items.title: Backpressure, load shedding, and graceful degradation
items.summary: A system under overload needs a way to say 'less work' before it spends all its resources failing.
objectives: Distinguish rate limits, concurrency limits, and queue bounds.
Choose which work to reject or degrade under overload.
Calculate how long a burst buffer takes to fill.

questions.prompt: Can a requests-per-second limit alone protect a dependency whose latency suddenly increases tenfold?
questions.answer: Not reliably. In-flight work can grow dramatically, so concurrency and waiting also need bounds.
questions.explanation: Not reliably. In-flight work can grow dramatically, so concurrency and waiting also need bounds.

questions.prompt: Why can a fallback make an outage worse?
questions.answer: The alternative path may be more expensive or have less capacity than the normal path.
questions.explanation: The alternative path may be more expensive or have less capacity than the normal path.

items.title: Service objectives and error budgets
items.summary: Reliability becomes useful when it describes what users can accomplish.
objectives: Define good and eligible events for an SLI.
Calculate an event-based error budget and burn rate.
Connect reliability measurements to operational decisions.

questions.prompt: For a 99.5% target and 200,000 eligible events, how many bad events are allowed?
Is an error budget permission to ignore all errors below the threshold?
questions.answer: No. It is a decision tool; severe correctness, security, or concentrated user failures may require action regardless of aggregate budget.
questions.explanation: No. It is a decision tool; severe correctness, security, or concentrated user failures may require action regardless of aggregate budget.

items.title: Logs, metrics, traces, and useful observability
items.summary: Observability means having evidence to explain behavior you did not predict in advance.
objectives: Choose signals that answer a concrete debugging question.
Propagate correlation across synchronous and queued work.
Control metric cardinality and telemetry sensitivity.

questions.prompt: Why should request IDs usually not be metric labels?
questions.answer: Their near-unbounded values multiply time series and storage cost; logs or traces are better suited to individual IDs.
questions.explanation: Their near-unbounded values multiply time series and storage cost; logs or traces are better suited to individual IDs.

questions.prompt: Does a fast acceptance endpoint prove a background workflow is fast?
questions.answer: No. Queue waiting and execution can dominate end-to-end latency after acceptance.
questions.explanation: No. Queue waiting and execution can dominate end-to-end latency after acceptance.

items.title: Performance testing that exposes bottlenecks
items.summary: A load test is an experiment with a question, a workload, and a pass condition.
objectives: Choose a workload model that matches user behavior.
Measure offered load as well as successful throughput.
Design a repeatable capacity and recovery experiment.

questions.prompt: Why can a constant-virtual-user test hide overload?
questions.answer: As responses slow, each virtual user sends fewer requests, reducing the offered arrival rate.
questions.explanation: As responses slow, each virtual user sends fewer requests, reducing the offered arrival rate.

questions.prompt: What must accompany a throughput result?
questions.answer: Workload assumptions, offered load, latency/error outcomes, environment, and relevant resource or dependency limits.
questions.explanation: Workload assumptions, offered load, latency/error outcomes, environment, and relevant resource or dependency limits.

items.title: Safe releases and database migrations
items.summary: During a rolling release, old and new application versions coexist.
objectives: Define a canary comparison and stop condition.
Plan an expand-migrate-contract schema change.
Identify what an application rollback cannot reverse.

questions.prompt: Does deploying the previous application image reverse a database migration?
questions.answer: No. Data and schema changes persist independently and may no longer be compatible.
questions.explanation: No. Data and schema changes persist independently and may no longer be compatible.

questions.prompt: Why validate a backfill before dropping the old field?
questions.answer: Missing, stale, or incorrectly transformed values can otherwise become permanent user-visible data loss.
questions.explanation: Missing, stale, or incorrectly transformed values can otherwise become permanent user-visible data loss.

items.title: Authentication, authorization, and tenant isolation
items.summary: Authentication answers who is making a request.
objectives: Separate identity verification from permission decisions.
Carry trusted tenant scope through every data path.
Test object-level authorization and isolation under pooling.

questions.prompt: Does an unguessable UUID authorize access?
questions.answer: No. It reduces guessing but is not a permission check.
questions.explanation: No. It reduces guessing but is not a permission check.

questions.prompt: Is enabling row-level security enough when the application connects as a superuser?
questions.answer: No. Superusers bypass row security; the role and policy configuration are part of the guarantee.
questions.explanation: No. Superusers bypass row security; the role and policy configuration are part of the guarantee.

items.title: Backups, restore drills, and disaster recovery
items.summary: A replica can quickly copy an accidental deletion.
objectives: Distinguish replication from recoverable backup history.
Specify recovery point and recovery time objectives.
Design a restore drill that verifies business invariants.

questions.prompt: Why is a current replica not a substitute for historical backups?
questions.answer: It may faithfully replicate destructive or corrupting changes.
questions.explanation: It may faithfully replicate destructive or corrupting changes.

questions.prompt: What makes an RTO claim credible?
questions.answer: A timed, representative recovery exercise including data restoration, validation, dependencies, and traffic restoration.
questions.explanation: A timed, representative recovery exercise including data restoration, validation, dependencies, and traffic restoration.

items.title: Consistency models and execution histories
items.summary: Consistency is a rule about which observations are allowed.
objectives: Evaluate a history against a declared consistency model.
Distinguish transaction isolation from real-time ordering.
Explain which operations must stop during a partition.

questions.prompt: Does serializability alone require a later transaction to reflect every earlier completed transaction in wall-clock order?
questions.answer: No. That real-time requirement belongs to strict serializability.
questions.explanation: No. That real-time requirement belongs to strict serializability.

questions.prompt: Can a stale read be legal when it overlaps a write?
questions.answer: Yes, under linearizability it may be ordered before that overlapping write; completed-before-started operations impose stronger constraints.
questions.explanation: Yes, under linearizability it may be ordered before that overlapping write; completed-before-started operations impose stronger constraints.

items.title: Consensus, leader changes, and membership
items.summary: Consensus gives replicas a shared decision order despite some failures.
objectives: Separate consensus safety from progress.
Explain quorum intersection and leader-log restrictions.
Plan membership changes without creating competing majorities.

questions.prompt: Does a timeout prove the leader is dead?
questions.answer: No. It may be slow or partitioned; elections and term rules must preserve safety despite false suspicions.
questions.explanation: No. It may be slow or partitioned; elections and term rules must preserve safety despite false suspicions.

questions.prompt: Why must membership changes be coordinated?
questions.answer: Independent old and new majorities can otherwise make conflicting decisions without intersecting.
questions.explanation: Independent old and new majorities can otherwise make conflicting decisions without intersecting.

items.title: Distributed transactions and atomic commitment
items.summary: A transaction spanning multiple authorities needs agreement about its outcome.
objectives: Trace prepare and decision phases of atomic commitment.
Explain the blocking risk of an uncertain prepared participant.
Separate atomic commit from isolation and consensus.

questions.prompt: Can a prepared participant safely abort solely because its timer expired?
questions.answer: Not if a commit decision may already exist; it must follow the protocol's recovery rules.
questions.explanation: Not if a commit decision may already exist; it must follow the protocol's recovery rules.

questions.prompt: Does consensus automatically turn arbitrary database writes into a distributed transaction?
questions.answer: No. Consensus orders agreed state; atomic commitment and isolation across participants require additional protocol design.
questions.explanation: No. Consensus orders agreed state; atomic commitment and isolation across participants require additional protocol design.

items.title: Clocks, leases, and fencing tokens
items.summary: A lease says an owner is valid for a bounded period under a particular time model.
objectives: Separate elapsed time, wall time, and causal ordering.
Construct a stale lease-holder failure timeline.
Place fencing checks at the resource that must be protected.

questions.prompt: Does a distributed lock physically stop an expired worker?
questions.answer: No. The worker may continue; the protected resource must reject stale authority.
questions.explanation: No. The worker may continue; the protected resource must reject stale authority.

questions.prompt: Does a monotonic clock order events on different machines?
questions.answer: No. Its useful guarantee concerns elapsed time within its local clock domain.
questions.explanation: No. Its useful guarantee concerns elapsed time within its local clock domain.

items.title: Multi-region replication and conflict resolution
items.summary: Putting data in several regions improves locality and recovery options, but also creates the question of who may decide a conflicting update.
objectives: Choose write ownership per invariant.
Explain the loss hidden by last-writer-wins convergence.
Apply a mergeable data type without claiming arbitrary invariant safety.

questions.prompt: Does eventual convergence mean no user update was lost?
questions.answer: No. A deterministic winner policy can converge after discarding a concurrent intent.
questions.explanation: No. A deterministic winner policy can converge after discarding a concurrent intent.

questions.prompt: Can a CRDT counter alone guarantee never selling more than ten seats?
questions.answer: No. Independent increments may exceed the business limit; coordination or a proven allocation scheme is needed.
questions.explanation: No. Independent increments may exceed the business limit; coordination or a proven allocation scheme is needed.

items.title: Stream processing, event time, and correctness
items.summary: A stream has no natural final page.
objectives: Separate event time from processing time and watermarks.
Define a late-data policy for a windowed result.
State the recovery boundary of an exactly-once processing claim.

questions.prompt: Does a watermark make later arrival of older events impossible?
questions.answer: No. It represents the processor's progress assumption; the system still needs a late-data policy.
questions.explanation: No. It represents the processor's progress assumption; the system still needs a late-data policy.

questions.prompt: Does restoring a checkpoint undo an email already sent by a sink?
questions.answer: No. External effects require their own transactional, idempotent, or compensating treatment.
questions.explanation: No. External effects require their own transactional, idempotent, or compensating treatment.

items.title: Design a ticket-booking system
items.summary: Build a reservation workflow whose correctness survives double clicks, expired holds, payment delays, and heavy contention.
objectives: Enforce exclusive ownership of a seat despite concurrent requests.
Model expiring holds and uncertain payment outcomes.
Protect the authoritative reservation path during a flash crowd.

questions.prompt: Can two users both see a seat as available without violating correctness?
questions.answer: Yes. The display may be stale; the authoritative claim and confirmation must still have one winner.
questions.explanation: Yes. The display may be stale; the authoritative claim and confirmation must still have one winner.

questions.prompt: Why not hold a database transaction open throughout payment?
questions.answer: A slow external call would retain locks/resources, and the transaction still cannot roll back a provider's independent effect.
questions.explanation: A slow external call would retain locks/resources, and the transaction still cannot roll back a provider's independent effect.

questions.prompt: What happens to a late successful payment after the seat is reassigned?
questions.answer: Reconcile and void/refund under an explicit workflow; do not issue a second ticket.
questions.explanation: Reconcile and void/refund under an explicit workflow; do not issue a second ticket.

criteria.evidence: Shows an enforceable uniqueness/conditional-update boundary.
Traces both winner orders without double confirmation.
Uses stable identity, reconciliation, and compensation.
Protects authoritative work and separates browsing freshness.
Uses durable workflow/outbox state and repeat-safe consumers.

architecture.builder_brief: Required reasoning: the cache is a display path; the database is the reservation authority; the external payment has a recoverable identity. Challenge distractor: confirming a booking directly from a cached available flag. Accept alternate architectures only if they enforce the same ownership and recovery rules.

items.title: Design a payment-processing workflow
items.summary: Design the application-side payment workflow around stable operation identity, durable state, and reconciliation.
objectives: Preserve one logical payment across retries and ambiguous responses.
Maintain an auditable balanced journal.
Reconcile provider state with local workflow and accounting state.

questions.prompt: Does a balanced journal prove the provider and application agree?
questions.answer: No. Entries can balance while being missing, duplicated under different identities, or assigned to the wrong business meaning.
questions.explanation: No. Entries can balance while being missing, duplicated under different identities, or assigned to the wrong business meaning.

questions.prompt: Can webhook arrival order be used as the authoritative payment sequence?
questions.answer: No. Delivery can be repeated or reordered; validate transitions and reconcile canonical state.
questions.explanation: No. Delivery can be repeated or reordered; validate transitions and reconcile canonical state.

questions.prompt: Why does a refund need its own operation identity?
questions.answer: It is a separate external effect that can also be retried or have an uncertain outcome.
questions.explanation: It is a separate external effect that can also be retried or have an uncertain outcome.

criteria.evidence: Scopes and retains logical operation identities correctly.
Checks balance and uniqueness within a durable transaction.
Explains uncertain charge/refund results and provider limits.
Verifies, durably accepts, and processes duplicate/reordered events.
Defines measurable discrepancy and repair workflows.

architecture.builder_brief: Required reasoning: webhook receipt is distinct from business processing; the provider effect lies outside the local transaction. Challenge distractor: mark every timed-out payment failed and issue a new operation key. Grade journal invariants and uncertainty handling, not provider brand choice.

items.title: Design a durable job scheduler
items.summary: Build a scheduler that can explain every accepted job through retries, stale workers, and leadership changes.
objectives: Separate scheduling, dispatch, execution, and effect guarantees.
Recover jobs after worker and scheduler failures.
Use fencing and tenant budgets without promising universal exactly-once execution.

questions.prompt: Can lease expiry guarantee that only one worker is running?
questions.answer: No. An old worker may be paused or partitioned and later resume.
questions.explanation: No. An old worker may be paused or partitioned and later resume.

questions.prompt: What should identify one recurring occurrence?
questions.answer: A stable schedule identity plus a precisely defined occurrence, independent of which scheduler discovers it.
questions.explanation: A stable schedule identity plus a precisely defined occurrence, independent of which scheduler discovers it.

questions.prompt: Does fencing a result row deduplicate every external effect?
questions.answer: No. Every affected destination needs a compatible idempotency or authority protocol.
questions.explanation: No. Every affected destination needs a compatible idempotency or authority protocol.

criteria.evidence: Deduplicates scheduling and dispatch independently.
Uses atomic epoch checks and traces stale-worker behavior.
States the limits of execution and effect guarantees.
Bounds tenant work, retries, and starvation.
Explains crash, cancellation, orphan, and version recovery.

architecture.builder_brief: Required reasoning: distinguish broker delivery from authoritative ownership and result publication. Challenge distractor: trust a worker's local clock and publish after any lease it once held. Accept queue-less implementations if they show equally durable claiming, bounded polling, and recovery.

items.title: Design search and autocomplete
items.summary: Design a search service that stays useful while its derived index lags, rebuilds, and handles repeated events.
objectives: Build a recoverable projection from authoritative content.
Define search freshness and deletion visibility.
Separate full-text relevance from prefix suggestions and authorization.

questions.prompt: Does source-database commit mean a document is immediately searchable?
questions.answer: No. Ingestion and search refresh introduce separate visibility stages.
questions.explanation: No. Ingestion and search refresh introduce separate visibility stages.

questions.prompt: Why keep version information on deletes?
questions.answer: A delayed update or snapshot replay must not resurrect a document deleted by a newer version.
questions.explanation: A delayed update or snapshot replay must not resurrect a document deleted by a newer version.

questions.prompt: Can autocomplete share the exact access policy of public search by assumption?
questions.answer: No. Suggestions can reveal private titles or sensitive queries and need their own explicit visibility controls.
questions.explanation: No. Suggestions can reveal private titles or sensitive queries and need their own explicit visibility controls.

criteria.evidence: Defines no-gap snapshot and change replay.
Handles stale updates, duplicates, and tombstones.
Separates relevance, filters, prefix behavior, and pagination.
Maintains privacy during lag and rebuild.
Measures freshness and bounds query/indexing load.

architecture.builder_brief: Required reasoning: search is a rebuildable projection with an explicit freshness contract. Challenge distractor: trust stale indexed visibility for every private result. Alternative indexes are acceptable when they demonstrate filtering, deletion, replay, and query limits.

items.title: Design a feature-flag service
items.summary: Build a flag system whose rollout decisions remain predictable when configuration distribution fails.
objectives: Separate flag administration from request-time evaluation.
Keep cohorts deterministic across clients and restarts.
Define safe behavior during stale or unavailable configuration.

questions.prompt: Will increasing a threshold preserve the old cohort if the rollout salt also changes?
questions.answer: Not generally. Changing the hash input reshuffles buckets.
questions.explanation: Not generally. Changing the hash input reshuffles buckets.

questions.prompt: Can a local flag cache guarantee immediate response to a kill switch during a partition?
questions.answer: No. A bounded guarantee needs an expiry or online protocol and a stated failure policy.
questions.explanation: No. A bounded guarantee needs an expiry or online protocol and a stated failure policy.

questions.prompt: Does enabling a feature flag grant permission to its API?
questions.answer: No. Authorization must independently enforce access.
questions.explanation: No. Authorization must independently enforce access.

criteria.evidence: Defines types, defaults, and authorization separation.
Handles atomic versions, gaps, and reconnect recovery.
Specifies stable identity, hashing, salt, and test vectors.
States stale-config and emergency-disable limits.
Provides audit, rollback, telemetry, and flag retirement.

architecture.builder_brief: Required reasoning: distinguish the control plane from evaluation and demonstrate safe defaults. Challenge distractor: fetch remote configuration synchronously for every local-mode evaluation without a deadline/fallback. Grade deterministic cohorts and stale-config behavior rather than a specific vendor.

items.title: Design a multi-region SaaS platform
items.summary: Design regional operation and failover around a precise authority model, measurable recovery targets, and tenant isolation.
objectives: Place write authority and data by tenant and invariant.
Recover regional service without creating competing writers.
Make latency, recovery, isolation, and cost trade-offs explicit.

questions.prompt: Does changing DNS establish a single writer?
questions.answer: No. Existing connections and partitioned old servers can continue; authority must be enforced at the write boundary.
questions.explanation: No. Existing connections and partitioned old servers can continue; authority must be enforced at the write boundary.

questions.prompt: Can the same RPO be assumed for every data class?
questions.answer: No. Replication, acknowledgement, retention, and recovery rules can differ by invariant and data class.
questions.explanation: No. Replication, acknowledgement, retention, and recovery rules can differ by invariant and data class.

questions.prompt: Is a globally reachable directory enough to make a service region-independent?
questions.answer: No. Its own quorum, data plane dependencies, identity services, keys, and recovery paths must survive the required failures.
questions.explanation: No. Its own quorum, data plane dependencies, identity services, keys, and recovery paths must survive the required failures.

criteria.evidence: Prevents conflicting writes during partition and failover.
Separates consistency and RPO by invariant and failure model.
Enforces scope and placement during routing/recovery.
Budgets failed-region load and replication overhead.
Defines measurable drills, failback, and honest unavailable states.

architecture.builder_brief: The diagram shows one illustrative home-region replication arrangement, not permission for all three replicas to write the same tenant simultaneously. Required reasoning: authority, replication, and routing each have explicit protocols. Challenge distractor: promote an async replica and update DNS without fencing the previous writer.
